classification.difficultyReason: Find an equilateral triangle's altitude using Pythagoras, then sum the areas of two triangular and three rectangular faces.

questions.mappingNote: Part a explicitly requires Pythagoras to find the triangular altitude. Part b applies the taught face-by-face surface-area method, using that altitude and the prism height of 12 cm.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines prism surface area as the sum of face areas. Page 3 Example 1b finds a missing triangular side using Pythagoras, calculates individual triangular and rectangular face areas, then sums them. Pages 4–5 cover cylinders and do not change the method for this prism.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find an equilateral triangle's altitude using Pythagoras, then sum the areas of two triangular and three rectangular faces.

classification.difficultyReason: Works backwards from the total area of six equal square faces to find the cube's side length.

questions.mappingNote: The rectangular-prism surface-area teaching and Example 1 support summing face areas. This question applies that method in reverse to a cube.
questions.methodNote: Find surface area by adding the areas of all faces. A cube has six equal square faces; reverse this calculation and take the positive square root to obtain a length.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Works backwards from the total area of six equal square faces to find the cube's side length.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute the radius and curved surface area into the cylinder formula and solve for height.

questions.mappingNote: This question reverses the taught curved-surface calculation to find height. The cylinder surface-area skill is the closest supplied catalogue match.
questions.methodNote: Page 4 derives curved surface area as circumference times height, 2πrh. Page 5 demonstrates substitution into this formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute the radius and curved surface area into the cylinder formula and solve for height.

classification.difficultyReason: Selects the surfaces of an open cylinder and rearranges the curved surface area formula to find height.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies the taught surface-by-surface method with one circular base because the lid is excluded. Part b substitutes the curved area and radius into 2πrh, then uses inverse operations to find height.
questions.methodNote: Add the areas of the actual surfaces. Page 4 derives curved surface area as 2πrh; page 5 Example 2 calculates curved and circular areas separately before adding them.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Selects the surfaces of an open cylinder and rearranges the curved surface area formula to find height.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the perpendicular height of an isosceles triangular cross-section using Pythagoras, then calculate prism volume without rounding the intermediate height.

questions.mappingNote: Part a obtains the triangular altitude using the equal sides and Pythagoras. Part b applies the triangular-prism method of Example 3b using that altitude and AD as the prism length. Supplied teaching pages do not demonstrate the prerequisite Pythagoras step.
questions.methodNote: Pages 6–7 establish prism volume as cross-sectional area multiplied by perpendicular prism height. Page 8 Example 3b substitutes the area of a triangular base into V=Ah.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find the perpendicular height of an isosceles triangular cross-section using Pythagoras, then calculate prism volume without rounding the intermediate height.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange the cylinder volume formula to find height and radius, retaining exact values until the requested rounding.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts use the taught cylinder volume formula with inverse operations: divide to find height in part a; divide and take the positive square root to find radius in part b. None of the supplied reuse candidates matches this complete task.
questions.methodNote: Pages 6–7 develop volume as base area multiplied by perpendicular height and give the cylinder formula V = πr²h. Page 8 Example 3d demonstrates substitution into that formula and retains π exactly.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange the cylinder volume formula to find height and radius, retaining exact values until the requested rounding.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply cube volume in reverse using one cube root, exact in the first case and one-decimal rounding in the second. No modelling choice or multi-method inference.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts ask for a dimension from a given volume. Part a has an exact integer cube root; part b requires a cube root rounded to one decimal place.
questions.methodNote: Pages 6–7 establish volume as base area multiplied by perpendicular height. Page 8 Example 3a substitutes the three rectangular-prism dimensions into this formula. For a cube this gives V = s³; taking the cube root reverses the calculation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply cube volume in reverse using one cube root, exact in the first case and one-decimal rounding in the second. No modelling choice or multi-method inference.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise two hidden contact squares at each join of three supplied cubes and the explicitly excluded largest base, then subtract from familiar cube face totals. Requires choosing exposed surfaces in a supplied composite, with no proof or unsupplied modelling.

questions.mappingNote: Apply the taught face-area method to three cubes, subtracting the covered contact regions and the explicitly excluded base. Composite surface area is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 teach surface area as the sum of face areas, using opposite rectangular face pairs. Page 8 repeats the face-area definition. Pages 4, 6 and 7 were inspected for context and concern cylinders or volume.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise two hidden contact squares at each join of three supplied cubes and the explicitly excluded largest base, then subtract from familiar cube face totals. Requires choosing exposed surfaces in a supplied composite, with no proof or unsupplied modelling.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine daily capacity, a composite pentagonal cross-section and Pythagoras’ theorem to determine the prism’s length.

questions.mappingNote: The task combines capacity demand, Pythagoras’ theorem, a composite cross-sectional area and inverse prism volume; volume and capacity problems is the closest primary skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 uses Pythagoras’ theorem to find a missing prism dimension. Pages 6–7 establish V = Ah, including polygonal bases decomposed into simpler areas. Page 8 Example 3 substitutes cross-sectional area and prism length into this formula. The question itself supplies the volume-to-capacity equivalence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine daily capacity, a composite pentagonal cross-section and Pythagoras’ theorem to determine the prism’s length.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer the square box dimensions from the cylinder diameter and subtract the cylinder volume from the box volume.

questions.mappingNote: The task combines cylinder and rectangular-prism volumes, infers the box base dimensions from a snug fit, and finds unused space by subtraction. The supplied reuse candidates have different givens and response requirements, so none is source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 teaches prism volume V = Ah. Page 7 develops cylinder volume V = πr²h. Page 8 Example 3 demonstrates substitution for rectangular prisms and cylinders, including converting diameter to radius. Page 4 establishes the cylinder centre marker.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer the square box dimensions from the cylinder diameter and subtract the cylinder volume from the box volume.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate a supplied right-triangular base area then substitute the explicitly perpendicular height into the taught pyramid formula. Routine two-formula calculation.

questions.mappingNote: Question 1 applies that same formula with a right-triangular base instead of the square base in Example 4. AC and BC give the triangular base area, and VA supplies the perpendicular height.
questions.methodNote: Page 12 establishes V=1/3 Ah using perpendicular height. Example 4 on page 13 substitutes base area and perpendicular height; page 14 repeats the volume formula in the Pyramids summary.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate a supplied right-triangular base area then substitute the explicitly perpendicular height into the taught pyramid formula. Routine two-formula calculation.

classification.difficultyReason: Four direct substitutions of given base area and height into V=Ah/3; sideways orientation does not add an algebraic or modelling method.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly apply the pyramid volume formula to a supplied base area and height. The sideways orientation in part d tests recognition that perpendicular height is independent of page orientation.
questions.methodNote: Page 12 derives V = one third × base area × perpendicular height. Example 4 on page 13 substitutes the base area and height and gives the volume in cubic units.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Four direct substitutions of given base area and height into V=Ah/3; sideways orientation does not add an algebraic or modelling method.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate the square base area, substitute the given height into V=Ah/3 and round one decimal. Familiar direct numerical application.

questions.mappingNote: This question applies the same square-pyramid volume method as Example 4, with decimal measurements and an explicit one-decimal-place rounding instruction.
questions.methodNote: Page 12 establishes V = one third of base area times perpendicular height. Example 4 on page 13 substitutes the square base dimensions and height into this formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate the square base area, substitute the given height into V=Ah/3 and round one decimal. Familiar direct numerical application.

classification.difficultyReason: Scaffolded calculation of a face height using Pythagoras, followed by triangular face area and total surface area.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 uses the same construction and calculation sequence as Example 5, with VO=12 cm and square side 10 cm. Its four parts explicitly scaffold each stage.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 identifies the centre-to-midpoint distance as half the square side, uses Pythagoras to find the triangular face height, calculates one triangular face area, then adds four equal face areas and the square base.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Scaffolded calculation of a face height using Pythagoras, followed by triangular face area and total surface area.

classification.difficultyReason: Find each triangular face height using Pythagoras, then combine four face areas and the square base.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts independently supply the base side and perpendicular height. Their reference to question 6 specifies a method rather than missing mathematical givens. Surface area of a right pyramid is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 finds the triangular face height using the perpendicular pyramid height and half the square base side in Pythagoras' theorem, then adds four triangular face areas and the square base. Question 6 provides the same scaffold.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find each triangular face height using Pythagoras, then combine four face areas and the square base.

classification.difficultyReason: Find two different triangular-face heights using Pythagoras, then combine the four triangular faces and rectangular base.

questions.mappingNote: Question 8 applies the same method to a rectangular base, requiring two distinct face heights and two pairs of triangular faces rather than four identical faces.
questions.methodNote: Example 5 finds a triangular-face height using a right triangle formed by the perpendicular pyramid height and the centre-to-midpoint distance, then adds the base and triangular-face areas.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find two different triangular-face heights using Pythagoras, then combine the four triangular faces and rectangular base.

classification.difficultyReason: Identifies right-angled faces in a pyramid whose vertex is above a base corner, finds edge lengths using Pythagoras, and sums unequal triangular face areas and the base.

questions.mappingNote: Question 9 places the apex above a base corner rather than the centre. Apply the same Pythagoras and face-area methods to the four right-angled triangular faces; their areas are not all equal.
questions.methodNote: Pages 13–14 distinguish perpendicular height from triangular-face height, use Pythagoras to find a required length, and calculate surface area by adding triangular faces and the base.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identifies right-angled faces in a pyramid whose vertex is above a base corner, finds edge lengths using Pythagoras, and sums unequal triangular face areas and the base.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify radius and slant height from each diagram, halve the diameter in part c, and substitute into the total surface area formula.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly assess total cone surface area; part c requires converting diameter to radius.
questions.methodNote: Example 6 adds curved surface area πrℓ and base area πr².

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify radius and slant height from each diagram, halve the diameter in part c, and substitute into the total surface area formula.

classification.difficultyReason: Two parts require finding slant height using Pythagoras before calculating total area.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b use that sequence; c directly substitutes the supplied slant height. Exact answers agree with the answer key.
questions.methodNote: Example 6b finds slant height using Pythagoras, then adds curved and base areas.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Two parts require finding slant height using Pythagoras before calculating total area.

classification.difficultyReason: Find slant height from curved area, then use Pythagoras to find perpendicular height.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly follows both stages of Example 7.
questions.methodNote: Example 7 solves πrℓ equal to the curved area, then uses h²+r²=ℓ² without rounding the intermediate length.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find slant height from curved area, then use Pythagoras to find perpendicular height.

classification.difficultyReason: The parts scaffold subtracting the base area, rearranging the curved area formula for slant height, and using Pythagoras for height while retaining intermediate precision.

questions.mappingNote: Combines the area decomposition of Example 6 with the inverse calculations of Example 7.
questions.methodNote: Examples 6 and 7 distinguish total and curved area, solve for slant height and apply Pythagoras for height.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: The parts scaffold subtracting the base area, rearranging the curved area formula for slant height, and using Pythagoras for height while retaining intermediate precision.

questions.methodNote: Use curved cone area πrℓ from pages 17–18 and cone volume from page 19.

questions.methodNote: Page 19 gives the cone-volume formula and demonstrates substituting a cone's radius and perpendicular height, retaining pi exactly.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate a cone's volume, apply a cost per cubic metre and round the final cost to the nearest dollar.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute a given radius into the sphere surface-area formula, halving the diameter first in parts c and d.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess sphere surface area. Parts a and b match Example 9a; parts c and d match Example 9b.
questions.methodNote: Page 22 defines the radius and teaches S = 4πr². Example 9 substitutes the radius, retains an exact multiple of π, then rounds to two decimal places; its diameter example first halves the diameter. Page 23 repeats the surface-area formula in the summary.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish the circular face, curved surface and total exposed surface of a solid hemisphere.

questions.mappingNote: Part a applies circular area; part b takes half the sphere surface area; part c adds both exposed surfaces. Surface area of a hemisphere is the directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 22 gives S = 4 pi r squared and demonstrates substitution, exact multiples of pi and final decimal approximation. Pages 17–18 separate base and curved areas before adding them. Page 23 repeats the sphere surface-area formula.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguish the circular face, curved surface and total exposed surface of a solid hemisphere.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange the sphere surface-area formula and take the positive square root, retaining precision until the final rounding.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses the sphere surface-area formula, reversed to find the radius; surface-area-sphere is the closest catalogue skill.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the exposed hemisphere surfaces, then rearrange the area formula to find the radius.

questions.methodNote: Page 22 gives the sphere surface area formula and substitution method. Halve that area for the curved hemisphere and add the circular base only when a material floor is present. classification.difficultyReason: Identify exposed surfaces, exclude internal joins, find a cone's slant height and account for a hemispherical cavity.

questions.mappingNote: For 5a halve the sphere area and add the exposed cylinder and base. For 5b infer the hemisphere radius from the height difference, find the cone slant height by Pythagoras and add curved areas. For 5c subtract the circular opening from prism area and add the curved hemisphere. Composite surface area is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Pages 17–18 teach curved cone area as πrℓ, separate base area, and Pythagoras for slant height. Page 22 teaches sphere area 4πr² and converting diameter to radius. Page 23 repeats the sphere area formula; its volume method is not needed here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify exposed surfaces, exclude internal joins, find a cone's slant height and account for a hemispherical cavity.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify radii from radius or diameter labels, apply the sphere volume formula and halve it for hemispheres.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c assess sphere volumes, with diameter conversion in c. Parts d–f assess hemisphere volumes, with diameter conversion in e and f. The hemisphere skill is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 22 defines the radius and shows how to distinguish radius from diameter. Page 23 supplies V = 4πr³/3 and Example 10 converts a diameter to a radius before substitution. A hemisphere uses half the sphere volume. Cone teaching on pages 17–18 is not needed for this question.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify radii from radius or diameter labels, apply the sphere volume formula and halve it for hemispheres.

classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange the taught sphere/hemisphere formula, take cube roots, then double unrounded radii and convert units with three distinct precision requirements. Familiar multistep inverse applications.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts reverse the sphere-volume relationship. Parts (b) and (c) then double the unrounded radius to find the diameter; part (c) first accounts for the hemispherical volume. Pages 7 and 19 provide earlier volume context; page 23 supplies the directly relevant method.
questions.methodNote: Page 23 states V=4πr³/3. Example 11 substitutes the volume, isolates r³, takes a cube root and converts centimetres to millimetres when requested. A hemisphere has half the corresponding sphere volume.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Rearrange the taught sphere/hemisphere formula, take cube roots, then double unrounded radii and convert units with three distinct precision requirements. Familiar multistep inverse applications.

questions.methodNote: Use the cylinder formula V=πr²h, cone formula V=πr²h/3 and sphere formula V=4πr³/3. A hemisphere has half the sphere volume. Substitute the radius, retain exact values and round the final volume.

questions.methodNote: Page 7 gives the cylinder formula V=πr²h. Page 23 gives V=4πr³/3 and Example 10 converts diameter to radius before substitution. Retain exact arithmetic until the requested final rounding.
